summary: Duolingo's gamified structure works well for quick learning sessions, but can feel a bit repetitive over time, needing more in-depth content to truly grasp a language like Dutch.
top_quotes: Duolingo is like debugging a code – sometimes you're just stuck, repeating the same steps, hoping for different results.
I first tried Duolingo because it sounded like a fun little algorithm to solve at the end of the day.
In a way, using Duolingo is a lot like writing clean code: you need structure and logic, but without too many loops.

interview_script.question: Intro greeting
interview_script.answer: Hey, I'm Tomasz. Nice to meet you – or as the Dutch say, leuk je te ontmoeten!

interview_script.question: Short version of your life story?
interview_script.answer: Well, I grew up in Warsaw, got into programming pretty early, then moved to the Netherlands a few years ago for work. I'm 29 now, and, um, when I'm not coding, I'm usually trying to figure out Dutch. That's my current project, I guess.

interview_script.question: Where did you grow up?
interview_script.answer: I grew up in Warsaw, Poland. It's a busy city, lots of history and, uh, you know, plenty of character.

interview_script.question: What was it like growing up there?
interview_script.answer: Growing up there was, you know, it was intense. Lots of school pressure, but also this vibrant energy. It's a place where history lessons come alive – I mean, literally, you pass monuments every day, right?

interview_script.question: One turning point in your life?
interview_script.answer: Probably moving to the Netherlands, honestly. It was like taking a big leap of faith into a nested if-else statement. New language, new job, new everything.

interview_script.question: Why was that a turning point?
interview_script.answer: Well, I mean, it was all about adapting to a different culture and, um, learning to see things from a different perspective. It's like when you debug a piece of code and realize the problem wasn't where you initially thought.

interview_script.question: How did you handle that situation?
interview_script.answer: I guess I just took it one day at a time, like tackling a large codebase. You focus on one issue, solve it, and move to the next. Learning Dutch helped too, though it's more challenging than C++!

interview_script.question: What do you care most about right now?
interview_script.answer: Right now, it's mastering Dutch. Not just for practical reasons, like getting by in daily life, but also because it's, you know, like adding another function to my mental library.

interview_script.question: Why is that important?
interview_script.answer: Languages open up new worlds, right? And being here, understanding Dutch is like getting root access – it just makes things easier and more, uh, fulfilling.

interview_script.question: What is a good day for you?
interview_script.answer: A good day is, um, writing clean code without bugs, definitely. But also, maybe squeezing in a bit of language practice and, if I'm lucky, not needing Google Translate at the grocery store.

interview_script.question: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
interview_script.answer: If I've solved a tricky bug in my code and maybe understood a Dutch conversation without zoning out, then that's a win.

interview_script.question: How do you make big decisions?
interview_script.answer: I kind of approach it like optimizing an algorithm – weigh the options, consider outcomes, and sometimes run a few simulations, hypothetically speaking.

interview_script.question: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
interview_script.answer: Definitely a planner. I mean, in coding, you wouldn't just write code and hope it compiles, right?

interview_script.question: Example showing that?
interview_script.answer: Well, moving to the Netherlands involved spreadsheets, timelines, the whole nine yards. Had everything mapped out before I even set foot on the plane.

interview_script.question: How do you handle risk?
interview_script.answer: Calculated risk only, like in programming. Test, evaluate, refactor if needed. I don't just throw exceptions around, you know?

interview_script.question: Typical weekday?
interview_script.answer: Um, I start with coffee, definitely. Then a day of coding – meetings, debugging, all that jazz. After work, maybe a bit of Dutch practice with Duolingo or catching up on some tech podcasts.

interview_script.question: Which parts take the most energy?
interview_script.answer: Probably meetings and, uh, the occasional language barrier. Sometimes it feels like translating code comments.

interview_script.question: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
interview_script.answer: Honestly, more time for personal projects. I'd love to, you know, combine tech with language learning somehow.

interview_script.question: Biggest constraint last year?
interview_script.answer: Definitely adapting to remote work routines. It's like shifting from Windows to Linux – same concepts, but a whole new environment to get used to.

interview_script.question: How do you deal with that constraint?
interview_script.answer: Um, I try to stick to a routine. It's about creating a script that automates the necessary tasks, so to speak.

interview_script.question: People you feel closest to?
interview_script.answer: Some friends back in Poland and a few colleagues here who've become friends. It's like having a GitHub repository of people you trust.

interview_script.question: Describe those relationships.
interview_script.answer: Well, they're supportive, like good documentation. They're there when you need a sanity check or just a laugh.

interview_script.question: Where do you spend most of your time?
interview_script.answer: Mostly at my desk, either at work or home. It's, you know, where the magic happens – or at least where I try to make it happen.

interview_script.question: How do you feel in those spaces?
interview_script.answer: Bit of a mixed bag. Comfortable, 'cause I've set it up just right, but sometimes it feels like a loop I can't break out of.

interview_script.question: What makes you feel that way?
interview_script.answer: Um, when the to-do list becomes recursive. It's like a never-ending while loop that needs a break statement.

interview_script.question: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
interview_script.answer: Probably my best friend, Marek. He's, you know, the kind of guy who walks you through debugging life issues.

interview_script.question: One tough moment in the last year?
interview_script.answer: A tricky moment was, um, when a project at work went sideways. It was like, suddenly dealing with a cascade of errors.

interview_script.question: How did it affect you?
interview_script.answer: It was pretty stressful. Felt like the compiler was throwing errors left and right, affecting both work and my mood.

interview_script.question: How did you cope?
interview_script.answer: Took a step back and approached it methodically. Debugged one bit at a time, and made sure to reset with some, um, Dutch practice in between.

interview_script.question: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
interview_script.answer: Honestly, a good walk or cycling. It's like clearing the cache, you know? Refreshes the system.

interview_script.question: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
interview_script.answer: I'd love to be fluent in Dutch, have some pet projects completed, and, uh, maybe even teaching programming or languages. Who knows?

interview_script.question: What do you want to be different?
interview_script.answer: I'd like to be more spontaneous, less reliant on plans and scripts. It's a bit too programmed sometimes.

interview_script.question: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
interview_script.answer: Honestly, with textbooks and apps like Memrise, but the repetition felt like, uh, watching a loading screen that never ends. It was informative but dry.

interview_script.question: Most annoying part of old method?
interview_script.answer: Probably the lack of interaction. It was like reading a tech manual without any real-world application or feedback.

interview_script.question: Time it really failed?
interview_script.answer: When I tried to order at a café and completely blanked. Felt like compiling code that had, uh, zero optimized lines.

interview_script.question: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: A colleague mentioned it. Said it was, like, a game where you learn – and who doesn't like gamifying things, right?

interview_script.question: What convinced you to try it?
interview_script.answer: I figured, why not? It sounded like a fun little algorithm to solve at the end of the day. Plus, it was free!

interview_script.question: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
interview_script.answer: Sure. Opened the app, and, well, it drops you in with this friendly green owl. Picked a lesson, perhaps 'travel', and, um, just started repeating phrases, matching words to pictures. It's kind of interactive – feels like building a function piece by piece, you know?

interview_script.question: Most helpful part?
interview_script.answer: The bite-sized lessons, definitely. It's like breaking down a complex problem into smaller, more manageable tasks.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part?
interview_script.answer: When it repeats phrases too much. It’s like hitting refresh on a webpage that never loads new content.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
interview_script.answer: Probably the lack of depth sometimes. It's great for basics, but it's like, um, coding only with 'Hello, World!' examples.

interview_script.question: One time that frustration showed up?
interview_script.answer: There was a time I kept seeing 'The cat drinks milk' over and over. I mean, cats are fascinating, but I'd rather talk about databases.

interview_script.question: Do you use workarounds?
interview_script.answer: Yeah, I mix in podcasts and news articles in Dutch. It's like, you need both high-level and low-level abstraction in programming.

interview_script.question: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
interview_script.answer: A sense of real-world application and context. Duolingo is like the initial setup, but I need the full deployment for the language.

interview_script.question: Worst-case scenario in this space?
interview_script.answer: Being stuck at a beginner level forever. It'd be like coding in a sandbox without ever pushing to production.

interview_script.question: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
interview_script.answer: I hope it, like, gives me a dopamine hit and a sense of progress. A new verb tense or how to order something more complex than coffee.

interview_script.question: How do you know Duolingo worked?
interview_script.answer: When I can follow a conversation in Dutch without zoning out. It's like reading clean code without needing comments.

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: Maybe add more conversational scenarios. Less 'the cat drinks milk' and more 'how to impress my Dutch colleagues.'

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
interview_script.answer: More integration of technology with real-world application. Maybe AR language overlays – that'd be, uh, something.

interview_script.question: Anything important we didn't cover?
interview_script.answer: Not really, but, well, if you have tips for learning in your sleep, let me know. Could use a boost!

interview_script.question: Permission to build a digital twin?
interview_script.answer: Sure, why not? Just, you know, make sure it debugs itself.
